facts.label: Hubble Space Telescope: mass (after the 2009 servicing mission)
facts.display: about 27,000 lb (12,250 kg); about 24,000 lb at launch

sources.title: NASA Science: A NASA Refresher on Hubble Facts for the 25th Anniversary (Goddard, 16 Apr 2015)
NASA Facts: Hubble Space Telescope - An Overview (fact sheet PDF)

facts.notes: NASA refresher: 'Hubble weighed about 24,000 pounds at launch and currently weighs about 27,000 pounds following the final servicing mission in 2009.' Its spec list: 'Post SM4: ~27,000 lbs. (~12,247 kg)', so 12,247 kg is NASA's own conversion. Fact sheet: 'Weighing about 27,000 pounds, the telescope is approximately the same size and weight as a school bus.' A NASA round figure, good to a few per cent. Input to energy_hubble_orbit_kinetic, not a rung. Skeptic: confirmed (and found NASA's 12,247 kg in the spec list).

facts.label: Hubble Space Telescope: orbital speed
facts.display: about 17,000 mph (27,300 km/h, 7.6 km/s) at 340 miles (547 km) up

sources.title: NASA Science: A NASA Refresher on Hubble Facts for the 25th Anniversary (Goddard, 16 Apr 2015)
NASA Facts: Hubble Space Telescope - An Overview (fact sheet PDF)

facts.notes: NASA refresher: 'Altitude of 340 miles (295 nautical miles, 547 km ... Time to Complete One Orbit: ~95 minutes Speed: ~17,000 mph (27,300 kph)'. Fact sheet: 'the speed of about 5 miles (8 km) per second' (rounder). 17,000 mph = 7,600 m/s; 27,300 km/h = 7,583 m/s. Check: circular-orbit speed sqrt(GM/r) at 547 km (GM = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2, R = 6,371 km) is 7,591 m/s. Speed relative to Earth's centre. Input to energy_hubble_orbit_kinetic, not a rung. Skeptic: confirmed; 547 km is the 2015 height, and Hubble has since sunk somewhat lower (skeptic's figure, not sourced), which raises the speed by under 0.3%.

facts.label: Hubble Space Telescope: kinetic energy (energy of motion) in orbit
facts.display: about 350 GJ (12,250 kg at about 7.6 km/s; about 85 t of TNT)

sources.title: NASA Science: A NASA Refresher on Hubble Facts for the 25th Anniversary (Goddard, 16 Apr 2015)
NASA Facts: Hubble Space Telescope - An Overview (fact sheet PDF)

facts.notes: KE = 1/2 m v^2 with m = 12,247 kg (energy_input_hubble_mass) and v = 7,600 m/s (energy_input_hubble_speed) = 3.54e11 J (84.5 t TNT). At the circular-orbit speed for 547 km (7,591 m/s): 3.53e11 J. NASA round inputs, so about +/-5%. Speed measured from Earth's centre; relative to the ground below it is up to about 5% lower (about 10% less energy). This is the energy to stop Hubble, or to bring it up to speed; lifting it to its height takes about 6.1e10 J more (17%), from GM m (1/R - 1/(R+h)). Skeptic: arithmetic confirmed; page phrase changed to say 'energy of motion', since 'the Hubble Space Telescope in orbit' does not explain itself.
facts.page_short: the Hubble Space Telescope's energy of motion in orbit

facts.label: Tianjin port explosions, 12 Aug 2015: total TNT-equivalent energy (official investigation)
facts.display: about 450 t TNT in all (1.9 TJ); the two main blasts about 15 t and 430 t

sources.title: State Council investigation team (Feb 2016): 天津港“8·12”瑞海公司危险品仓库特别重大火灾爆炸事故调查报告 (official report, gov.cn PDF), pp. 17-18

facts.notes: Report p. 17: '第一次爆炸的能量约为 15 吨 TNT 当量，第二次爆炸的能量约为 430 吨 TNT 当量' (from simulations by the State Key Laboratory of Explosion Science and Technology: first blast about 15 t TNT, second about 430 t). p. 18: '确定本次事故中爆炸总能量约为 450 吨 TNT 当量' (allowing for several smaller blasts, total about 450 t TNT). 450 t x 4.184e9 J = 1.88e12 J. No range given. The report also lists 800 t of ammonium nitrate in storage. An academic estimate of about 500 t (Fang et al. 2017) was seen only in a search summary, not opened. Alternative to Beirut for the 1e12 J slot (one official number, not rough; less known in the West). Skeptic: confirmed word for word; citation corrected from p. 17 to pp. 17-18.
facts.who_when: Chinese State Council investigation team, Feb 2016

facts.label: Beirut port explosion, 4 Aug 2020: TNT-equivalent yield
facts.display: about 0.3-1.1 kt TNT in published estimates (0.13-2 kt at the extremes); 0.5 kt (2.1 TJ) used, Rigby et al.'s best estimate

sources.title: Rigby et al. (2020) Preliminary yield estimation of the 2020 Beirut explosion using video footage from social media, Shock Waves 30:671-675, doi:10.1007/s00193-020-00970-z (published version, White Rose repository)
Pilger et al. (2021) Yield estimation of the 2020 Beirut explosion using open access waveform and remote sensing data, Scientific Reports 11:14144, doi:10.1038/s41598-021-93690-y (PMC8266808)

facts.notes: Rigby abstract: 'The best estimate and reasonable upper limit ... are 0.50 kt TNT and 1.12 kt TNT, respectively'; about 2,750 t of ammonium nitrate. Pilger: yield 'determined within 0.13 to 2 kt TNT'; video studies give 'the range from 0.3 to 1.12 kt TNT'; infrasound (LANL relation) 'about 0.5 kt TNT ... (0.14-1.12 kt TNT)'; near-source damage 'best explained by a yield of 0.8-1.1 kt TNT'; seismic 0.13-0.34 kt is 'a lower bound'. Value 0.50 kt, Rigby's published best estimate (Pilger's infrasound figure agrees). low/high: the published video range, 0.3-1.12 kt. 1 kt = 4.184e12 J. High/value = 2.2, so rough multiple only. Skeptic: the earlier 0.75 kt was a chosen midpoint, not a published estimate, and the 0.5-1.1 kt range left out lower published estimates; value, range and display corrected.
facts.who_when: Rigby et al. 2020; Pilger et al. 2021

facts.label: Halifax explosion, 6 Dec 1917: TNT-equivalent energy
facts.display: about 2.9 kt TNT (12 TJ); approximate, no published error bar

sources.title: Parks Canada backgrounder: The Halifax Explosion (Government of Canada, 2016)
NATO Munitions Safety Information Analysis Center (MSIAC): accident poster 07, Halifax, Nova Scotia, 6 Dec 1917
Wikipedia: Halifax Explosion (cites Ruffman & Howell 1994, Ground Zero, p. 276, for 2.9 kt)

facts.notes: Parks Canada: 'With a force equivalent to 2.9 kilotons of TNT' (read only through a fetch tool; curl fails). MSIAC: 'The SS Mont Blanc was carrying 2.3 million kg of explosives, the majority of which was picric acid' and 'The energy released was estimated to be roughly equivalent to 2.9 million kg of TNT.' Both trace to Ruffman & Howell (eds) 1994, Ground Zero, p. 276 (via Wikipedia; book not opened). No error bar published; treat as approximate. 2.9 x 4.184e12 = 1.21e13 J. Skeptic: confirmed; 'verified' is defensible (a Canadian government agency and NATO MSIAC), though both summarise one book; the cargo size supports roughly 2.5-3 kt (skeptic's reasoning, not sourced). Not the recommended rung: the Space Station's energy of motion sits within 4% of it, is better constrained and is not a disaster.
facts.who_when: Ruffman & Howell 1994, via Parks Canada 2016 and NATO MSIAC

facts.label: International Space Station: mass

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

facts.notes: NASA: 'Mass: 925,335 pounds (419,725 kilograms)'. 925,335 lb x 0.45359237 = 419,725 kg. The station's mass changes a little as vehicles dock and leave; the page gives no date for the figure. Input to energy_iss_orbit_kinetic, not a rung. Skeptic: confirmed.

facts.label: International Space Station: orbital speed
facts.display: about 7.7 km/s (from NASA's 90-minute orbit); NASA rounds it to 'five miles per second' (8.0 km/s); about 7.66 km/s at its real height

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

facts.notes: NASA: crew 'traveling at a speed of five miles per second, orbiting Earth about every 90 minutes'; 'In 24 hours, the space station makes 16 orbits of Earth'. Circular orbit: v = (2 pi GM / T)^(1/3) with T = 5,400 s and GM = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2 gives 7,741 m/s. high_si: NASA's rounder 'five miles per second' (8,047 m/s). low_si: circular speed at about 420 km, 7,660 m/s (physics; the height is not sourced). Skeptic: the 90-minute period is rounded and implies an orbit only about 280 km up, so 7,741 m/s is about 1% high; low_si added. Speed relative to Earth's centre. Input to energy_iss_orbit_kinetic, not a rung.

facts.label: International Space Station: kinetic energy (energy of motion) in orbit
facts.display: about 12-14 TJ (420 t at 7.7-8.0 km/s; about 3 kt of TNT); 12.6 TJ used

sources.title: NASA: Space Station Facts and Figures

facts.notes: KE = 1/2 m v^2 with m = 419,725 kg (energy_input_iss_mass) and v = 7,741 m/s (energy_input_iss_speed) = 1.258e13 J (3.0 kt TNT). With NASA's 'five miles per second': 1.359e13 J (high_si); at the realistic 7.66 km/s: 1.231e13 J (low_si). Good to about 10%. Speed relative to Earth's centre. Within 4% of the Halifax explosion (energy_halifax_explosion_1917), which it replaces as the 1e13 J rung: better constrained, known worldwide, not a disaster. Skeptic: arithmetic confirmed; low_si added and display widened to 12-14 TJ; page phrase says 'energy of motion'.
facts.page_short: the International Space Station's energy of motion in orbit

facts.label: Hiroshima (Little Boy) yield
facts.display: 15 kt (LANL: outside limits +/-20%, so 12-18 kt) = 6.3 x 10^13 J; DS02 dosimetry: 16 +/- 2 kt

sources.title: Malik (1985) Yields of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki nuclear explosions, LANL report LA-8819, OSTI 1489669 (abstract)
DOE/NV-209 Rev 16 (Sept 2015) United States Nuclear Tests, July 1945 through September 1992, NNSA Nevada Field Office, PDF p. 15
RERF DS02 report, Chapter 1 Bomb Parameters (Kerr, Young, Cullings, Christy)

facts.notes: Update of the existing fact (same key and values): status claimed -> verified, now from LANL/DOE/RERF sources instead of Wikipedia. Malik (OSTI abstract): 'Hiroshima 15 kt Nagasaki 21 kt The outside limits of uncertainties in these values are believed to be 20 percent for Hiroshima and 10 percent for Nagasaki.' DOE/NV-209 (PDF p. 15): 'The first combat detonation was a 15-kt weapon airdropped August 6, 1945, at Hiroshima, Japan.' DS02 Ch. 1: 'The calculated yield for the Hiroshima device is currently 16 +/- 2 kt', with 14 and 18 kt at 99% confidence. All within 12-18 kt. Skeptic: all three confirmed; DS02's 99% range added.

facts.label: Sedan nuclear cratering test, 6 Jul 1962 (Nevada): yield
facts.display: 104 kt = 4.4 x 10^14 J; dug a crater 1,280 ft (390 m) wide and 320 ft (98 m) deep

sources.title: NNSS fact sheet: Sedan Crater (NNSS-SEDN-U-0047, Rev 01)
DOE/NV-209 Rev 16 (Sept 2015) United States Nuclear Tests (Sedan entry, PDF p. 41)

facts.notes: NNSS: 'an excavation experiment using a 104-kiloton thermonuclear device. The test, detonated 635 feet underground ... displaced about 12 million tons of earth, creating a crater 1,280 feet in diameter and 320 feet deep.' DOE/NV-209 (PDF p. 41): Sedan, 07/06/1962, Crater, Plowshare, 104 kt; the by-name list and text agree. One official value, no range. 104 x 4.184e12 = 4.35e14 J. A peaceful earth-moving experiment, no casualties. Skeptic: confirmed, but obscure as a yardstick (a general reader won't know it); usable only with a gloss, hence the long phrase. Not a recommended rung: Hiroshima (up to 10x) and Chelyabinsk (down to 10%) already cover its decade; kept as the fallback if a tighter step is wanted there.
facts.who_when: US AEC test; DOE/NNSA 2015, NNSS fact sheet
facts.page_short: the 1962 Sedan nuclear test, which dug a crater 390 m wide

facts.label: Seismic energy radiated by a magnitude 7 earthquake (rough)
facts.display: about 2 x 10^15 J of shaking (USGS formulas give 0.7-2.1 x 10^15 J); real quakes vary more

sources.title: USGS: Earthquake Magnitude, Energy Release, and Shaking Intensity
USGS: Magnitude Types (Me entry)

facts.notes: USGS energy page: 'log E = 5.24 + 1.44Mw' (units not stated; joules fits) -> 2.1e15 J at M7. Magnitude Types: 'log10E = 11.8 + 1.5MS' with E 'in ergs' -> 2.0e15 J at M7, the relation the page's seismic model uses (seismic_gutenberg_richter_energy_magnitude). Same entry: 'Me = 2/3 log10E - 2.9'; read with E in joules, Me 7 means 7.1e14 J (low_si). Radiated shaking only, a small part of all the energy released. Skeptic: formulas confirmed; the value sits at the top of the range (geometric middle 1.2e15 J), and the spread is only the formulas' disagreement: real M7 quakes vary more in what they radiate (about 5x; general seismology, not checked). Rough multiple only. Not a recommended rung (Chelyabinsk covers 1e15 J).
facts.page_short: the shaking from a magnitude 7 earthquake

facts.label: Chelyabinsk meteor airburst, 15 Feb 2013: energy
facts.display: about 500 +/- 100 kt TNT (1.7-2.5 PJ); NASA's fireball table: 441 kt

sources.title: Brown et al. (2013) A 500-kiloton airburst over Chelyabinsk and an enhanced hazard from small impactors, Nature 503:238-241, doi:10.1038/nature12741
NASA/JPL CNEOS Fireball Data API, 2013-02-15 event

facts.notes: Brown et al. abstract: 'the airburst of an asteroid about 19 metres (17 to 20 metres) in diameter ... estimated to have an energy equivalent of approximately 500 (+/-100) kilotons of trinitrotoluene (TNT, where 1 kiloton of TNT = 4.185x10^12 joules)'. Nature's editor summary: '400 to 600 kilotons of TNT'. JPL fireball API row: 2013-02-15 03:20:26, radiated energy 37500 (x10^10 J), impact-e 441 (kt), altitude 23.3 km, speed 18.6 km/s; 441 kt sits inside 400-600 kt. Value 500 kt x 4.184e12 J = 2.09e15 J (Brown's 4.185e12 changes it by 0.02%). About +/-20%. Skeptic: all confirmed; the Popova et al. 2013 abstract (PubMed) gives no energy figure.
facts.who_when: Brown et al. 2013 (Nature); NASA JPL CNEOS

facts.label: Hoover Dam: electricity generated in an average year
facts.display: about 4 billion kWh in an average year (14 PJ); 1947-2008 average 4.2 billion kWh

sources.title: US Bureau of Reclamation: Hoover Dam - Frequently Asked Questions: Hydropower (last updated 1 Aug 2018)

facts.notes: USBR: 'Hoover Dam generates, on average, about 4 billion kilowatt-hours of hydroelectric power each year for use in Nevada, Arizona, and California - enough to serve 1.3 million people.' Also: 'The average annual net generation for Hoover Powerplant for 1947 through 2008 was about 4.2 billion kilowatt-hours' (1999-2008: also about 4.2 billion). Single years vary: maximum 10,348,020,500 kWh in 1984 (3.7e16 J), minimum since 1940 2,648,224,700 kWh in 1956 (9.5e15 J). 4.0e9 kWh x 3.6e6 J/kWh = 1.44e16 J; low/high are USBR's two stated averages. The page's data run only to 2008; drought-era output since was not checked. Skeptic: confirmed word for word; page phrase changed to 'an average year'.
facts.who_when: US Bureau of Reclamation (FAQ, data to 2008)
facts.page_short: an average year of the Hoover Dam's electricity

facts.label: Castle Bravo yield (28 Feb 1954 GMT; 1 Mar local)

sources.title: DOE/NV-209 Rev 16 (Sept 2015) United States Nuclear Tests, July 1945 through September 1992, NNSA Nevada Field Office (Bravo entries, PDF pp. 30 and 91)
Nuclear Weapon Archive: Operation Castle

facts.notes: Update of the existing fact (same key and value): status claimed -> verified. DOE/NV-209 Rev 16, the official US test list the earlier research could not retrieve, PDF p. 30: 'Bravo / 44 Experimental thermonuclear device 02/28/1954 LANL Bikini Atoll ---- Surface 18:45:00.00 ... Weapons Related 15 Mt'. NWA: '18:45:00.0 28 February 1954 (GMT) 06:45:00.0 1 March 1954 (local) ... Yield: 15 Mt'; NWA lists 10 Mt of it as fission. Sources differ on the predicted yield (NWA 6 Mt, Wikipedia 5 Mt); that does not affect the 15 Mt actual. 15,000 x 4.184e12 = 6.28e16 J. Skeptic: value and status confirmed; page citation corrected from PDF p. 60 to p. 91 (the by-name listing).

rungs.page_short: the Hubble Space Telescope's energy of motion in orbit
the International Space Station's energy of motion in orbit
an average year of the Hoover Dam's electricity

gaps: None in this band. With the recommended rungs, the steps from the MOAB (4.6e10 J, explosive band) to the Tsar Bomba (2.1e17 J, geophysical band) are: Hubble's energy of motion 7.7x, Beirut 5.9x, the Space Station's energy of motion 6.0x, Hiroshima 5.0x, Chelyabinsk 33x, an average Hoover Dam year 6.9x, Castle Bravo 4.4x, the Tsar Bomba 3.3x. One decade has no rung inside it: 1e14 to 1e15 J (Hiroshima 6.3e13 to Chelyabinsk 2.1e15, 33x). It is covered from both sides (at most 10x Hiroshima up to 6.3e14 J, at least 10% of Chelyabinsk from 2.1e14 J; worst case about 6x Hiroshima or 17% of Chelyabinsk), but it is the widest step. Fallback for it: the Sedan test (4.4e14 J, verified, obscure, needs its gloss). On firm (non-rough) rungs only, Hubble to the Space Station is 36x, still covered from both sides. If the MOAB (still 'claimed', Wikipedia only) is dropped, the A380 (1.8e10 J, explosive band) to Hubble is 20x, also covered from both sides.
